nodes.name: Electrochemical Iridium Loading on NiSe
nodes.procedure: Highly dispersed Ir was electrochemically loaded onto Ni-based precursor NiSe using H₂IrCl₆ as the Ir precursor. During electrochemical loading, Se is leached out and replaced by OH⁻, confirming the reconstruction of the catalyst into a hydroxide phase and resulting in the formation of an oxygen-dominated surface. The Ir content on PC-Ir/NiSe was determined to be ~0.6 wt% by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES). High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images of PC-Ir/NiSe did not show any visible particles or clusters, indicating a high dispersion of Ir species on NiSe. Aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-HAADF-STEM) clearly showed a high dispersion of Ir single atoms on NiSe, visible as bright spots in the lattice scattering, which was further supported by atomic-level elemental mappings.
nodes.source_text: By electrochemically loading highly dispersed Ir onto Ni-based precursors such as NiSe, we achieve the coupling of Ir loading and catalyst reconstruction, leading to the formation of an oxygen-dominant surface... The Ir content on PC-Ir/NiSe was determined to be ~0.6 wt% by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES, Table S1)... Aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-HAADF-STEM) clearly showed a high dispersion of Ir single atoms on NiSe, visible as bright spots in the lattice scattering (Figure 1d), which was further supported by atomic-level elemental mappings (Figure 1e).

nodes.name: Electrochemical Activation of Ir/NiSe
nodes.procedure: Following electrochemical iridium loading, the catalyst undergoes electrochemical activation. During this activation, the signals of M-OH and lattice oxygen further increase, and Se 3d regions remain almost undetectable, confirming the full surface reconstruction into the active NiOOH-Se phase. XPS analysis shows that after electrochemical activation, the O 1s spectrum reveals a significant increase in the intensity of M-OH species and lattice oxygen, while the Se 3d signal becomes nearly undetectable.
nodes.source_text: Following electrochemical activation, the signals of M-OH and lattice oxygen further increase, and Se 3d regions remain almost undetectable, confirming the full surface reconstruction.

nodes.name: Electrochemical Iridium Loading and Activation on NiSOH
nodes.procedure: Highly dispersed Ir was electrochemically loaded onto Ni-based precursor NiSOH using H₂IrCl₆ as the Ir precursor, similar to the procedure for NiSe loading. The precatalyst PC-Ir/NiSOH undergoes electrochemical activation, resulting in the formation of the Ir/NiOOH-S₁ active phase through surface reconstruction.
nodes.source_text: we prepared NiSOH, NiS₂ and Ni(OH)₂ loaded with highly dispersed Ir (Figures S18-S24, the precatalyst is referred to as PC-NiSOH, PC-NiS₂, and PC-Ni(OH)₂, while the real-catalytic material is designated as NiOOH-S₁, NiOOH-S₂, and NiOOH, respectively)

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM images of PC-Ir/NiSe show no visible particles or clusters, indicating high dispersion of Ir species on NiSe.
nodes.evidence_snippet: High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images of PC-Ir/NiSe did not show any visible particles or clusters (Figure S2), indicating a high dispersion of Ir species on NiSe.

properties.description: High-resolution TEM showing nanoparticles dispersed on support material

nodes.characterization_summary: AC-HAADF-STEM clearly shows high dispersion of Ir single atoms on NiSe, visible as bright spots in the lattice scattering, further supported by atomic-level elemental mappings showing Ir, Ni, O, and Se distribution.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-HAADF-STEM) clearly showed a high dispersion of Ir single atoms on NiSe, visible as bright spots in the lattice scattering (Figure 1d), which was further supported by atomic-level elemental mappings (Figure 1e).

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS analysis of PC-NiSe shows Se 3d peak at 54.9 eV attributed to Se-Ni bonding, indicating alloyed state. Ni 2p shows pronounced Ni⁰ doublet peaks at 852.5 and 870.5 eV. Secondary Se 3d peak at 59.0 eV confirms oxidized selenium species (SeOₓ) on surface.
nodes.evidence_snippet: XPS analysis of the Se 3d spectrum for PC-NiSe shows a peak at 54.9 eV, which can be attributed to Se-Ni bonding (Figure S3), indicating that PC-NiSe predominantly exists in an alloyed state, matching well with the Ni 2p XPS spectrum, where pronounced Ni⁰ doublet peaks are observed at 852.5 and 870.5 eV, respectively. A secondary peak of Se 3d at 59.0 eV confirms the presence of an oxidized selenium species (SeOₓ) on the surface.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS O 1s spectrum of PC-Ir/NiSe after electrochemical iridium loading reveals significant increase in M-OH species and lattice oxygen intensity, while Se 3d signal becomes nearly undetectable, indicating Se leaching and replacement by OH⁻ with formation of oxygen-dominated surface.
nodes.evidence_snippet: After electrochemical iridium loading, the O 1s spectrum reveals a significant increase in the intensity of M-OH species and lattice oxygen, while the Se 3d signal becomes nearly undetectable (Figure S4-S5). This suggests that during electrodeposition, Se is leached out and replaced by OH⁻, confirming the reconstruction of the catalyst into a hydroxide phase and resulting in the formation of an oxygen-dominated surface.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS analysis following electrochemical activation shows further increase in M-OH and lattice oxygen signals, with Se 3d regions remaining almost undetectable, confirming full surface reconstruction.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Following electrochemical activation, the signals of M-OH and lattice oxygen further increase, and Se 3d regions remain almost undetectable, confirming the full surface reconstruction.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman spectroscopy of Ir/NiOOH-Se in 1 M NaOH at 1.32 V vs RHE shows α-Ni(OH)₂ phase with peaks at 447 and 490 cm⁻¹ corresponding to ν(Ni-OH) and ν(Ni-O) vibrational modes.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Recorded in 1 M NaOH and 1 M NaOH + 0.2 M NaCl at 1.32 V vs RHE, the catalyst exhibited the α-Ni(OH)₂ phase, with Raman peaks at 447 and 490 cm⁻¹ corresponding to the ν(Ni-OH) and ν(Ni-O) vibrational modes of α-Ni(OH)₂ (Figure 2d and Figure S9).

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman spectroscopy of Ir/NiOOH-Se at 0.4 M NaCl shows transition to γ-NiOOH phase with peaks at 474 cm⁻¹ and 553 cm⁻¹ corresponding to δ(Ni-O) and ν(Ni-O) modes, indicating reduced formation barrier of γ-NiOOH active phase.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As the Cl⁻ concentration increased to 0.4 M, the catalyst predominantly transitioned to the γ-NiOOH phase, characterized by Raman peaks at 474 cm⁻¹ and 553 cm⁻¹, corresponding to the δ(Ni-O) and ν(Ni-O) modes of γ-NiOOH, respectively, indicating a reduced formation barrier of γ-NiOOH active phase over Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl (Figure 2e and f).

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman spectroscopy shows vibrational band at 658 cm⁻¹ corresponding to ε(Ir-O), confirming that Ir is bridging to Ni via oxygen.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Furthermore, the vibrational band observed at 658 cm⁻¹ corresponding to ε(Ir-O), confirms that Ir is bridging to Ni via oxygen.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman comparison of Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl and Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH shows significantly stronger 474 cm⁻¹ peak in Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl, with I₄₇₄/₅₅₃ ratio increasing from 2.0 to 2.4 as potential increased from 1.47 to 1.57 V vs RHE, indicating more γ-NiOOH formation on Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The results showed a significantly stronger 474 cm⁻¹ peak in Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl compared to that in Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH (Figure 2g and h), with the I₄₇₄/₅₅₃ ratio increasing from 2.0 to 2.4 as the potential increased from 1.47 to 1.57 V vs RHE.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman spectroscopy of Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH shows I₄₇₄/₅₅₃ ratio remaining stable at 1.3 over the examined potential range from 1.47 to 1.57 V vs RHE.
nodes.evidence_snippet: However, for Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH, the I₄₇₄/₅₅₃ ratio remained stable at 1.3 over the examined potential range (Figure 2i).

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando ¹⁸O-labeled Raman measurements of Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl show δ(Ni-¹⁸O) vibration at 454 cm⁻¹ at OCV, which disappears in 15 s at 1.32 V vs RHE, with concurrent emergence of δ(Ni-¹⁶O) and ν(Ni-¹⁶O) peaks at 474 and 553 cm⁻¹, indicating rapid involvement of lattice oxygen in OER.
nodes.evidence_snippet: At OCV, a Raman shift at 454 cm⁻¹ attributable to δ(Ni-¹⁸O) was observed, confirming successful labeling of lattice oxygen by ¹⁸O. Subsequently, when the applied anodic voltage increased to 1.32 V vs RHE, the δ(Ni-¹⁸O) vibration band disappeared in 15 s, and concurrently two new vibration peaks emerged at 474 cm⁻¹ and 553 cm⁻¹ which could be assigned to δ(Ni-¹⁶O) and ν(Ni-¹⁶O

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando ¹⁸O-labeled Raman measurements of Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH show ν(Ni-¹⁸O) vibration at 535 cm⁻¹ at OCV, shifting slowly to ν(Ni-¹⁶O) at 553 cm⁻¹ as potential increased from 1.29 to 1.42 V vs RHE, with δ(Ni-¹⁸O) appearing gradually at 454 cm⁻¹ and shifting to δ(Ni-¹⁶O) at 474 cm⁻¹ at 1.45 V vs RHE, indicating higher activation energy barrier for lattice oxygen.
nodes.evidence_snippet: At OCV, the ν(Ni-¹⁸O) vibration band was detected at 535 cm⁻¹ over ¹⁸O-labeled Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH; however, the shift from ν(Ni-¹⁸O) to ν(Ni-¹⁶O) at 553 cm⁻¹ occurred slowly as the applied anodic potential increased from 1.29 to 1.42 V vs RHE. Meanwhile, the δ(Ni-¹⁸O) vibration band at 454 cm⁻¹ appeared gradually as the applied anodic potential rose to 1.35 V vs RHE... Subsequently, this vibration mode shifted to δ(Ni-¹⁶O) at 474 cm⁻¹ as the applied anodic potential increased to 1.45 V vs RHE.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman spectroscopy of Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH shows characteristic Raman shift of Ir=O-H₂O at 750 cm⁻¹, considered as the main OER active site for Ir-based catalysts following the AEM mechanism.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Additionally, unlike Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl, Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH exhibited a characteristic Raman shift of Ir=O-H₂O at 750 cm⁻¹ (Figure 3b), which is considered as the main OER active site for Ir-based catalysts following the AEM mechanism.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman spectroscopy shows ε(Ir-O) vibration at 663 cm⁻¹ in both Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl and Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH samples, with no Raman shift after ¹⁸O labeling, indicating that lattice oxygen of Ir-O-Ni did not participate in OER and the electron-withdrawing chain remains intact.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Importantly, the ε(Ir-O) vibration at 663 cm⁻¹, representing Ir-O coordination, showed no Raman shift in both samples after ¹⁸O labeling, indicating that the lattice oxygen of Ir-O-Ni did not participate in the OER and the reconstruction process.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando ¹⁸O-labeling DEMS measurements of Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl show significant ³⁴O₂ and ³⁶O₂ signals in both i-t and LSV tests, with ³⁴O₂/³²O₂ ratio of 0.53 (LSV) and 0.57 (i-t), demonstrating involvement of lattice oxygen in OER.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The results showed that for ¹⁸O-labeled Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl, significant ³⁴O₂ and ³⁶O₂ signals were detected in both the i-t (1.7 V vs RHE) and LSV test (from 1.1 to 1.7 V vs RHE), demonstrating the involvement of lattice oxygen in OER (Figure 3c and d). The ³⁴O₂/³²O₂ ratio reached 0.53 (from LSV test) and 0.57 (from i-t test) over Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando ¹⁸O-labeling DEMS measurements of Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH show ³⁴O₂/³²O₂ ratio of 0.44 (LSV) and 0.51 (i-t), significantly lower than Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl, indicating less involvement of lattice oxygen in OER.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The ³⁴O₂/³²O₂ ratio reached 0.53 (from LSV test) and 0.57 (from i-t test) over Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl, significantly higher than that over Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH (0.44 from LSV test and 0.51 from i-t test).

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando ¹⁸O-labeling DEMS measurements of Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl at higher potential (1.9 V vs RHE) show ³⁴O₂/³²O₂ and ³⁶O₂/³²O₂ ratios significantly higher than at 1.7 V vs RHE, rising from 0.53 to 0.7 and from 0.2 to 0.8 respectively, indicating stable and effective LOM pathway at high anodic potentials.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Additionally, at higher potential (1.9 V vs RHE), the ³⁴O₂/³²O₂ and ³⁶O₂/³²O₂ ratio measured over Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl were significantly higher than those measured at 1.7 V vs RHE, rising from 0.53 to 0.7 and from 0.2 to 0.8, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman measurements show both Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl and Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH exhibit Ir-Cl coordination under OCV, attributed to chlorinated Ir salt (H₂IrCl₆) used in electrochemical Ir loading.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The results showed that both Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl and Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH exhibited Ir-Cl coordination under OCV (Figure 3f,g), which was attributed to the chlorinated Ir salt (H₂IrCl₆) used in electrochemical Ir loading.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman measurements show that as potential increased to 1.57 V vs RHE, Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl maintains Cl⁻ adsorption equilibrium with Ir due to abundant Cl⁻ in electrolyte (0.5 M NaCl), while Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH shows Ir-Cl coordination replaced by OH⁻ as potential increased from OCV to 1.57 V vs RHE.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As the potential increased to 1.57 V vs RHE, over Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl, the abundant Cl⁻ in the electrolyte (0.5 M NaCl) allowed Cl⁻ to competitively adsorb with OH⁻ on the Ir sites, established a Cl⁻ adsorption equilibrium with Ir (Figure 3f). In contrast, over Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH, Ir-Cl coordination was only observed at OCV, which was gradually replaced by OH⁻ in the alkaline electrolyte as the anodic potential increased from OCV to 1.57 V vs RHE.

nodes.characterization_summary: Chronoamperometric curves at 10 mA/cm² show Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH undergoes dynamic coordination reconstruction in first 0-300 s with Ir-Cl replaced by Ir-OH, stabilizing at 1.54 V vs RHE. Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl shows continuous activity improvement after surface reconstruction (within 300 s), stabilizing at 1.4 V vs RHE.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The chronoamperometric curves recorded at 10 mA/cm² further demonstrated the reconstruction and coordination regulation processes in different electrolytes (Figure 2j). For Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH, a dynamic coordination reconstruction occurred in the first 0-300 s, during which the Ir-Cl coordination was replaced by Ir-OH. Afterward, the OER proceeded stably at near 1.54 V vs RHE. In contrast, the OER activity of Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl continuously increased after surface reconstruction (within 300 s), which was ultimately stabilized at 1.4 V vs RHE.

nodes.characterization_summary: LSV measurements with TMA⁺ chemical probe show Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl exhibits pronounced shift of oxidation peak to positive potential (+97 mV) and reduction peak to negative potential (-95 mV) with substantial decrease in OER activity, providing evidence that Ir-Cl coordination activates lattice oxygen and facilitates formation of *O₂²⁻ species.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 3h demonstrated that the strong interaction between Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl and TMA⁺ resulted in a pronounced shift of the oxidation peak to the positive potential (+97 mV) and the reduction peak to the negative potential (-95 mV) along with a substantial decrease in OER activity.

nodes.characterization_summary: LSV measurements with TMA⁺ chemical probe show Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH exhibits oxidation peak shift of only +36 mV with reduction peak largely unaffected, indicating OER catalyzed mainly following AEM pathway.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In contrast, in the presence of TMA⁺, the oxidation peak of Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH shifted by only +36 mV and the reduction peak remained largely unaffected (Figures S15 and S16), indicating that Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH catalyzed OER mainly following an AEM pathway.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS analysis of Ir 4f shows binding energy of Ir in Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl shifted by +0.48 eV compared to Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH, indicating higher oxidation state of Ir in Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Moreover, XPS analysis of Ir revealed that the binding energy of Ir in Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl shifted by +0.48 eV compared to that in Ir/NiOOH-Se@OH, indicating a higher oxidation state of Ir in Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl (Figure 3j and Figure S17).

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS analysis of Ni 2p shows Ni in Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl after reaction displays nearly unchanged valence state compared to as-prepared Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl, indicating reversible valence behavior of Ni critical for maintaining long-term operational stability.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Meanwhile, the Ni in Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl after reaction displayed a nearly unchanged valence state as compared to that in the as-prepared Ir/NiOOH-Se@Cl (Figure 3k), suggesting that Ni could be oxidized to +4 during OER and elastically recover to its starting valence state after the reaction.

nodes.characterization_summary: LSV measurements show Ir/NiOOH-S₁@Cl exhibits superior OER activity compared to Ir/NiOOH-S₁@OH, with overpotential at 100 mA cm⁻² being 85 mV lower, reducing energy consumption in alkaline seawater by 18.5%.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The results demonstrated that Ir/NiOOH-S₁@Cl and Ir/NiOOH-S₂@Cl also exhibited superior OER activity compared to Ir/NiOOH-S₁@OH and Ir/NiOOH-S₂@OH (Figure 4b and Figure S18). Notably, the overpotential of Ir/NiOOH-S₁@Cl at 100 mA cm⁻² was 85 mV lower than that of Ir/NiOOH-S₁@OH, reducing energy consumption in alkaline seawater by 18.5%.

nodes.characterization_summary: LSV measurements show Ir/NiOOH-S₂@Cl exhibits superior OER activity compared to Ir/NiOOH-S₂@OH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The results demonstrated that Ir/NiOOH-S₁@Cl and Ir/NiOOH-S₂@Cl also exhibited superior OER activity compared to Ir/NiOOH-S
